journeys.title: Faith, Character and Responsibility
journeys.aim: A sincere Muslim learns to connect belief, repentance and justice without judging the hidden hearts of others.

lessons.title: When Faith Becomes a Choice
story: The new school term began with a question on the academy noticeboard: WHAT DOES BELIEF CHANGE WHEN NOBODY IS WATCHING? Akhlaq had a quick answer. “It changes everything.” Sir Zameer smiled. “Then tell us about one choice, not a slogan.”

At break, the team found that the library book-return sheet had been completed incorrectly. A box of borrowed books was missing from the record, and the exhibition would look more successful if no one mentioned it. Mohsin suggested fixing the numbers quietly tomorrow. Imaan wanted the record corrected before the report was printed.

“Will people say our team is careless?” Akhlaq asked. “They might,” Imaan replied. “But they will certainly be misled if we hide what happened.” The children checked the books and changed the number. No one received applause. In fact, the librarian simply thanked them and asked them to organise the records better.

That evening, Salaam spoke about how Imaan belongs to the heart, while the Qur’an calls believers toward good action. “No one can examine another person’s sincerity from a classroom form,” he said. “But each of us is responsible for what we knowingly choose.” Akhlaq wrote a quieter answer to the original question: “When I believe Allah knows my actions, I have a reason to be honest even when honesty is inconvenient.”

teaching.text: The master manuscript connects Imaan, worship and character. The intention behind an act matters, but we cannot claim to know another person's inner sincerity. Faith does not become a competition between classmates. The Qur’an commands justice even when it is difficult (4:135), and Sūrah al-ʿAṣr links faith with good deeds, truth and patient encouragement. The hadith about intentions teaches us to examine our own purpose, not to appoint ourselves judges of other hearts. A mistake does not mean every good action has become worthless; a learner can correct the act and seek Allah’s forgiveness. We should distinguish what Islam requires from mere popularity, and learn to repair an error without hiding it under religious language.

questions.q: What does Imaan include?
questions.a: Sincere belief, which should guide our choices and duties.

questions.q: Can classmates measure one another’s sincerity?
questions.a: No. Allah knows hearts; we judge our own actions and follow proper outward rules.

questions.q: Why correct an inaccurate record?
questions.a: Because people have a right to truthful information.

questions.q: What may a person do after making a mistake?
questions.a: Admit it, correct harm, seek forgiveness and improve.

reflect: Which recent choice was difficult because the truthful option might embarrass me?

scenario: A group asks you to leave an error in its report because the teacher will not notice. What should you say, and how will you help fix it?
decide.feedback: Suggest checking the evidence together and correcting the record politely. Do not insult anyone’s Imaan.

lessons.title: A Mistake Is Not the End of the Road
story: An academy poster competition ended with a disagreement. Akhlaq had used an illustration from Mohsina’s notebook without asking. The poster was attractive, but Mohsina noticed the drawing as soon as it was displayed. “I spent two evenings making that,” she told him. “You could have asked.”

Akhlaq wanted to say that he had helped the whole team, so nobody should complain. When he returned home, Salamah listened without excusing what he had done. “You can be pleased with the team’s success and still recognise that another person’s right was ignored,” she said.

The next morning Akhlaq asked the teacher to pause the display. He apologised to Mohsina, removed the drawing and offered to add her name if she chose to give permission. She decided that the poster could keep the drawing with proper credit. Akhlaq felt relief, but not because the embarrassment had disappeared. He had finally dealt with what he could repair.

Sheikh Uncle later explained that Allah’s mercy should fill a person with hope. “Hope does not mean planning to repeat the wrong,” he said. “And when a wrong involves another person, a private prayer does not erase the duty to address their right.” The children wrote three words above their new work: STOP, RETURN, REPAIR.

teaching.text: Chapter 21 teaches the boundaries of belief, wrongdoing and repentance. The Qur’an’s call not to despair of Allah’s mercy (39:53) must not be misunderstood as permission to persist deliberately in harm. Repentance involves recognising and leaving wrongdoing, regretting it and resolving not to return. Where another person's right has been violated, restitution or an appropriate apology is also important. The master text treats shirk, disbelief and their consequences with scholarly care; children should not casually apply grave religious labels to themselves or anyone else. Some harms require responsible adult intervention. Forgiveness can be sought from Allah while action is taken in the world to stop harm and make amends.

questions.q: What does Tawbah mean?
questions.a: Sincerely turning back to Allah from wrongdoing.

questions.q: Does repentance allow us to keep hurting people?
questions.a: No. Sincere repentance means leaving the wrong.

questions.q: What is one way to repair harm?
questions.a: Return property, correct false claims or apologise appropriately.

questions.q: Who judges the hidden sincerity of repentance?
questions.a: Allah.

reflect: Do I sometimes want an apology to end a problem without changing my behaviour?

scenario: You shared a friend’s work without permission and now feel guilty. Is saying “I am sorry” enough if the work is still displayed under your name?
decide.feedback: Apologise, correct the credit or remove the work, and ask permission. Let the affected person have a fair choice.

lessons.title: The Danger of Judging Hearts
story: During a group task a pupil missed the lunchtime prayer because of a private family matter. One classmate began whispering that the pupil did not care about Islam. Akhlaq almost repeated the comment before Imaan asked, “Do we know why the pupil was absent?”

Sir Zameer stopped the conversation. “We have a duty to learn about prayer and encourage it correctly,” he said, “but a missing explanation is not proof of someone’s inner belief.” The class did not interrogate the pupil. Instead, they finished the school assignment and asked the teacher whether a more accessible prayer arrangement was needed for those with special circumstances.

That night Dadi Jaan reminded the siblings that the book’s sections on Kufr, Shirk and Bidʿah teach serious matters, not playground insults. A student who hears a difficult word should seek its scholarly definition and context rather than attach it to a person in anger.

Mohsin suggested a new exhibition rule: “Do not spread religious accusations you cannot support.” The children added a second rule: “If you see actual harm or danger, tell a responsible adult.” They discovered that caution does not mean avoiding responsibility. It means using truth, knowledge and justice together.

teaching.text: The master Chapter 21 explains that religious terms have precise meanings and that judgments about named individuals demand knowledge and proper authority. A sin should not automatically be treated as departure from Islam. Chapter 17 introduces honoured Companions and righteous servants without authorising claims that we can observe hearts. Qur’an 49:6 commands care with reports, while 49:12 warns against suspicion and backbiting. Children should learn distinctions between evaluating a public action, seeking help for danger, and claiming to know someone’s hidden spiritual standing. Never use “religious correction” to justify humiliation, exclusion or bullying.

questions.q: Is every sin the same as disbelief?
questions.a: No. Serious theological judgments have specific conditions and distinctions.

questions.q: May children declare classmates outside Islam?
questions.a: No. They should not make such judgments.

questions.q: What should we do with an unverified accusation?
questions.a: Avoid spreading it, check responsibly and consult trusted adults.

questions.q: What if the situation involves harm?
questions.a: Seek appropriate help from a trustworthy adult.

reflect: When have I repeated a label without knowing its full meaning?

scenario: A group wants to exclude a pupil because someone has questioned the pupil’s faith. What is a just response?
decide.feedback: Do not repeat the accusation or exclude the pupil. Inform an appropriate teacher and use respectful, verified information.

journeys.aim: We distinguish revealed belief from observation and learn to ask thoughtful questions without inventing answers.

lessons.title: Allah Is Eternal and Needs Nothing
story: The academy’s science room had lost power during a presentation. The projector needed electricity, the plants on the windowsill needed water, and the children needed lunch before their afternoon lessons. Akhlaq drew arrows between each object and what helped it function.

“Everything on the chart needs something,” he observed. Imaan added that people need care, food and air. “Does that mean Allah needs a larger source of power?” she asked, not because she believed it, but because the chart seemed to have no place to stop.

Sheikh Uncle closed the notebook gently. “The chart is about created things. We cannot place Allah on it as another machine or plant. The Qur’an teaches that creation depends on Him, while He is free of need.”

The children returned to the classroom and labelled their poster carefully: CREATED THINGS DEPEND. They placed a separate Qur’anic reference alongside it rather than attempting to draw Allah. When Akhlaq told the younger pupils what he had learned, he did not pretend the poster explained Allah’s Being. He said, “The things around us help us recognise dependence. Revelation teaches us who Allah is.”
The short answer was more accurate than his first clever diagram.

teaching.text: The original Chapter 11 uses the term Wājib al-Wujūd: Allah’s existence is not supplied by another and does not depend upon a cause or provider. “Necessary” does not mean that some outside force makes Him exist. The Qur’an teaches that Allah is the First and the Last (57:3), that human beings need Allah while He needs nothing (35:15), and that nothing is comparable to Him (42:11). Words such as Qidam, Azalī and Abadī describe His eternity. An analogy about a lamp, computer or tree is a reminder of created dependence, not a physical model of Allah or a complete philosophical demonstration. Learners should affirm the revelation and refrain from imagining God in the shape of an object.

questions.q: What does Wājib al-Wujūd mean in this lesson?
questions.a: Allah exists independently and does not receive existence from another.

questions.q: Does Allah need food or power like created beings?
questions.a: No. Allah is unlike creation and free of need.

questions.q: Which Sūrah stresses that none is comparable to Allah?
questions.a: Sūrah al-Ikhlāṣ.

questions.q: Why is a machine diagram an imperfect analogy?
questions.a: It describes created dependence, not Allah’s divine Being.

reflect: What does recognising my dependence teach me about gratitude and humility?

scenario: A pupil draws Allah as an enormous lightbulb to explain divine power. How can you respond without humiliating the pupil?
decide.feedback: Explain respectfully that Allah is not like created objects. Use the Qur’anic words instead of a picture of Allah.

lessons.title: Creator, Causes and Careful Reasoning
story: Sir Zameer offered the class a box of wooden wheels, string and cardboard. Each team had to build a small moving model. Mohsin made a cart, but it would not roll. Akhlaq found that the wheel was attached too tightly; once loosened, the cart moved.

“Now we know the cause of the problem,” said Mohsin. A pupil asked whether every question could be solved in the same way: find a loose screw or a missing part. Sir Zameer explained that investigation of how a mechanism works differs from the question of why the world exists at all.

Later Akhlaq asked, “If we explain a storm, a tree or a machine, have we explained away Allah?” Dadi Jaan invited him to remember Chapter 12 of their larger book. Observing regular causes is useful and truthful. Belief in Allah as Creator asks about the existence and dependence of the entire created order, not just a missing stage in a scientific explanation.

At the next exhibition rehearsal, Imaan wrote two questions side by side: HOW DOES THIS WORK? WHY DOES A DEPENDENT WORLD EXIST? She refused to declare them identical, even though both were worth studying.

teaching.text: The master manuscript introduces reasoning about created things, dependence and contingency while warning against pretending a simple analogy resolves every philosophical issue. Qur’an 52:35–36 calls people to reflect on their origin, and 2:164 points to signs in the world. The basic Islamic claim is that creation does not exist independently of Allah. Scientific and everyday causal accounts are real explanations within creation; they do not by themselves answer the metaphysical question of ultimate existence. Learners should ask for evidence, identify which question is being asked, and avoid slogan answers. It is acceptable to say, “I need to study this argument more carefully.”

questions.q: What does an ordinary causal explanation describe?
questions.a: How one event or mechanism is connected with another within the world.

questions.q: What does belief in Allah as Creator affirm?
questions.a: That all creation ultimately depends on Allah.

questions.q: Does identifying a natural process automatically deny the Creator?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Must every philosophical argument fit a one-line reply?
questions.a: No. Hard questions may need patient study.

reflect: Which question am I asking: how something works, or why the whole created world depends?

scenario: A friend says, “Science explains rain, so no believer should study weather.” What could you say?
decide.feedback: Explain that studying natural processes and believing in Allah’s creation are not opposites.

lessons.title: Science Is a Way of Studying Creation
story: The school water-cycle display returned for another year. This time the older pupils planned an experiment comparing how quickly water evaporated in sunlight and in shade. Akhlaq predicted the sunny cup would lose more. Imaan suggested marking the water levels and checking them at the same time.

After a day, the sunny container seemed lower, but Mohsina noticed that it was a different shape. “If our containers are not alike, the comparison may mislead us,” she said. The team restarted with matching containers.
“Does restarting mean we failed?” Mohsin asked. Sir Zameer answered, “Science improves when we correct a method. It does not become trustworthy because we refuse to admit a flaw.”

Later the children read the Qur’anic invitation to reflect on the heavens and earth. Dadi reminded them that the Qur’an is guidance, not an excuse to invent a modern scientific detail for every verse. They could observe rainfall carefully and also express gratitude to Allah without forcing either statement into a false competition.
Their new display included the words OBSERVE, TEST, CORRECT and GIVE THANKS. It was a better scientific project and a more honest learning experience.

teaching.text: Chapter 13 is a new explanatory expansion of the original Taʿleem-ul-Islam’s belief foundation. Science studies natural processes through evidence, measurement and testable explanations. Questions about divine creation are not solved merely by describing a mechanism. Learners should not claim that each scientific finding is directly predicted by a verse, or that a changing scientific model is identical to Revelation. The Qur’an encourages thoughtful attention to the natural world (3:190), while properly conducted science includes revising conclusions when better evidence appears. Muslim scientists and other scholars should be credited accurately, without exaggerated claims. Respectful discussion is possible without turning a science lesson into a fight.

questions.q: What is one feature of scientific inquiry?
questions.a: Careful observation or testing against evidence.

questions.q: Can a scientific explanation be revised?
questions.a: Yes, when the evidence supports revision.

questions.q: Is the Qur’an merely a laboratory manual?
questions.a: No. It is revelation and guidance.

questions.q: What attitude is shared by good learning in all subjects?
questions.a: Honesty about evidence and limits.

reflect: When have I defended a conclusion just because it was mine?

scenario: The first test did not support your prediction. A team member wants you to change the measurements. What would you do?
decide.feedback: Keep the measurements honest, investigate the method and repeat the test if appropriate.

lessons.title: Hard Questions Deserve Thoughtful Answers
story: A message appeared on the academy discussion board: “If people disagree about religion, asking questions must be forbidden.” Akhlaq was surprised. He liked asking questions, but he had seen debates become cruel. He asked Sir Zameer whether questions were dangerous.

“Questions can be sincere, careless or designed to provoke,” the teacher replied. “Our task is to understand what is actually being asked, respond with knowledge, and avoid insult.” He handed the class four short comments, each asking a different question: about Allah’s existence, about a verse, about a difficult personal event, and about a rumour posted online.

Imaan noticed that one question needed textual explanation, another needed philosophical study, a third needed compassion, and the rumour needed verification. No single memorised answer would help every person.

At home, Dadi encouraged the children to list questions they were still studying. “Writing ‘I do not know yet’ can be a sign of responsibility,” she said. Akhlaq crossed out an answer he had written too confidently. For the first time, he felt pleased to leave a blank line for a qualified teacher.

teaching.text: Chapter 20 examines questions raised by atheism and modern thought, including arguments about the Creator, suffering, morality and reason. For ages 11–12 the goal is not adversarial debate. Teach the child to identify the kind of claim, state core Muslim beliefs clearly, ask what evidence would be relevant, and recognise when further scholarly study is needed. Qur’an 16:125 instructs inviting with wisdom and good exhortation. A child should never be shamed for a sincere question or expected to answer every objection immediately. Respond to distress with care; a philosophical argument is not a replacement for help with suffering.

questions.q: Is a sincere question automatically wrongdoing?
questions.a: No. Ask respectfully and seek reliable knowledge.

questions.q: What should a learner say when uncertain?
questions.a: “I do not know yet; let us check a sound source.”

questions.q: How does Qur’an 16:125 shape discussion?
questions.a: With wisdom and respectful teaching.

questions.q: Are all difficult questions of the same kind?
questions.a: No. Some concern evidence, others meaning or personal distress.

reflect: Do I listen closely to a person’s question before answering?

scenario: An online clip mocks a student for asking about divine decree. Should you join the mockery or reply?
decide.feedback: Do not amplify the humiliation; encourage a respectful question and qualified explanation.

lessons.title: Qadar: Trust Without Giving Up Responsibility
story: Akhlaq had promised to prepare the school equipment list but forgot. When the exhibition arrived, two tables were missing. “It was written,” he told Mohsin. Imaan raised an eyebrow. “You were given a task. Did you try to finish it?”

The teacher asked the children to separate two questions: what Allah knows and decrees, and what responsibility a person has for a choice. People do not possess knowledge of the unseen. Akhlaq had known the deadline and could have asked for help, but he had postponed the work.

Instead of arguing, he phoned the caretaker with permission, arranged replacement tables and wrote a reminder for future tasks. He also apologised. Later Dadi explained that belief in Qadar does not mean refusing to plan, learn or repair mistakes. We ask Allah for help and use the appropriate means He has placed within our reach.

Mohsina added another example: a person who becomes ill has not failed to trust Allah by seeing a doctor. The class connected trust with responsible action, rather than confusing patience with passivity. Akhlaq finally changed the title of his notes from NOTHING IS MY DECISION to MY CHOICES STILL MATTER.

teaching.text: The master Chapter 18 treats divine decree, Allah’s knowledge and human responsibility together. Muslims believe Allah knows and decrees all things. This does not make people morally free to injure others or neglect duties. Allah calls people to make choices and holds them accountable within their ability. We should distinguish matters outside our control from actions we can choose, and use prayer, counsel, preparation and lawful means. Avoid simplistic statements that assign every difficult event to a person’s wrongdoing. The ultimate details of Qadar exceed a child’s complete understanding; the practical lesson is trust joined with effort and humility.

questions.q: What is Qadar?
questions.a: Belief in Allah’s decree and complete knowledge.

questions.q: Does Qadar excuse dishonesty?
questions.a: No. People remain accountable for voluntary actions.

questions.q: May we plan and seek medical help?
questions.a: Yes. Taking appropriate means is part of responsibility.

questions.q: Can we know all of Allah’s hidden wisdom?
questions.a: No.

reflect: What was outside my control today, and what was a real choice I could make?

scenario: You forgot a shared responsibility and blame Qadar. What would a better response be?
decide.feedback: Admit the neglect, apologise, try to repair the result and use a better plan next time.

lessons.title: When Hardship Meets Compassion
story: One of the team members had been away because a relative was unwell. Akhlaq suggested presenting a cheerful song to make the pupil feel better. Imaan wondered whether the family wanted a public show. Salamah advised the children to ask their teacher how best to support the pupil without asking for private medical information.

They quietly completed the missing class notes and offered help when the pupil returned. Nobody asked for explanations in front of the class. After school, Akhlaq told Dadi he found it confusing that some good people suffered. Dadi replied that Islam does not promise believers an easy life without sadness. Their learning about Qadar could not be used to explain the particular reason for another family’s hardship.
“Should we say they must be patient and stop talking?” he asked. “No,” Dadi said. “A sad person may make duʿāʾ, cry, rest and seek help. Compassion does not require silence.”

When the pupil returned, the team greeted them normally and offered the notes. The pupil thanked them and chose not to discuss the absence. Akhlaq had learned that hope can appear as ordinary, respectful assistance rather than a dramatic speech.

teaching.text: Chapter 18 discusses suffering alongside Allah’s knowledge, mercy and the duty of responsible action. Chapter 19 introduces the Hereafter without making worldly hardship a public test of anyone’s faith. A Muslim can seek Allah’s help and turn to trusted people at the same time. Never promise a specific worldly outcome or attribute a particular tragedy to a supposed personal sin. Offering practical help, protecting privacy and connecting a struggling child to appropriate adults may be more beneficial than an abstract answer. Compassion and sound theology should work together, not compete.

questions.q: Does strong faith mean never feeling sad?
questions.a: No. Sadness and reliance upon Allah can coexist.

questions.q: May someone seek counselling or medical care?

questions.q: Can we know why a particular family suffers?
questions.a: Not unless a sound source establishes it; we should not guess.

questions.q: What is one form of respectful help?
questions.a: Offer a useful task or support without pressuring disclosure.

reflect: When does my advice help someone, and when might listening be kinder?

scenario: A pupil returns after a private family crisis. Your friends want details. What is the considerate choice?
decide.feedback: Respect privacy, offer help and avoid speculation or pressure.

journeys.title: Revelation and Trustworthy Guidance
journeys.aim: We learn why source-checking and humility matter when learning religion or passing a teaching to others.

lessons.title: Reading Religious Sources Responsibly
story: Akhlaq was designing a display titled WORDS OF THE PROPHET ﷺ. He had copied a famous sentence from a decorative poster because it sounded beautiful. Imaan asked for its source. “It is on hundreds of websites,” he replied. Sheikh Uncle reminded him that repetition on many screens is not proof of accurate attribution.

They checked with a teacher and found that the poster did not provide a reliable reference. Rather than announcing that every copy was false, they removed the quotation until it could be verified. In its place they used a verified Qur’anic passage with its Sūrah and verse number and labelled the explanation as an English meaning.

Mohsin added a modern story about a classroom promise and asked whether it could appear beside the verse. “Yes,” Imaan said, “but label it as our own illustration, not something that happened to a Prophet.” The exhibit grew clearer as the children learned four labels: REVELATION, HADITH, EXPLANATION and FICTIONAL APPLICATION.
When a younger pupil visited the display, Akhlaq showed how a short reference can prevent a great misunderstanding. He liked the result, even without the original eye-catching quotation.

teaching.text: The master chapters explain the Qur’an as Revelation, the Messenger ﷺ as the bearer of authoritative guidance, and the responsibility to understand reliable sources. A Qur’anic translation conveys the meaning but is not a replacement for the Arabic Revelation. Hadith reports must be assessed through qualified scholarship, and a paraphrase must not be presented as verbatim prophetic speech. Classical Tafsīr is explanation grounded in scholarship; the fictional Imaan & Akhlaq stories are modern applications. A mature learner should ask: Who said this? Where is it recorded? Is the quotation exact? What does the source mean in context?

questions.q: Is an English translation identical to the Arabic Qur’an?
questions.a: No. It communicates the meaning of the Arabic Revelation.

questions.q: Does a viral quotation automatically become an authentic Hadith?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: May a fictional story be used as a lesson?
questions.a: Yes, if clearly separate from sacred history and Revelation.

questions.q: What should we do before attributing words to the Prophet ﷺ?
questions.a: Verify with a reliable source or qualified teacher.

reflect: What do I do when a beautiful quotation lacks a reference?

scenario: Your group wants to add a social-media hadith to a class poster but cannot verify it. What is the correct next step?
decide.feedback: Pause the attribution, seek verified sources and do not fill the gap by guessing.

lessons.title: Guidance, Scholarship and Respectful Difference
story: Two pupils at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy prepared separate prayer diagrams. Their hand positions did not look exactly alike. A third pupil announced that one diagram must prove the other child’s family was wrong about Islam.

Sir Zameer asked which authorised books the diagrams followed. The children discovered they knew much less about Fiqh than they thought. The teacher explained that recognised Sunni scholars sometimes differ after studying evidence through established methods. Their task was not to invent rulings from a photograph or to insult worshippers.

Imaan suggested a clear heading for their practical instruction: HANAFI METHOD TAUGHT IN OUR COURSE. Mohsin added a note that other recognised schools have evidence-based teachings, to be studied accurately with a qualified teacher. The group kept its practical sequence consistent rather than combining whichever opinion felt easiest.

At home, Salaam encouraged Akhlaq to respect the Companions, scholars and authentic texts without confusing any human scholar with the infallibility of Revelation. “Honouring a scholar includes learning carefully,” he said. “It does not mean pretending every question is simple.” Akhlaq finally saw why asking for guidance is different from losing confidence.

teaching.text: The master Chapter 22 introduces juristic categories, while Chapters 17 and 16 explain religious transmission and authority. The Hanafi school is the foundation of this student curriculum. Other recognised Sunni schools have methodologies and positions that cannot be summarised fairly as “one is strict and another is easy.” Learners should distinguish a shared obligation from a difference in classification or application. They should avoid legal shopping merely to escape duties and seek qualified guidance when a personal case is not covered by a simple textbook example. Scholarly disagreement must be studied with adab, not used to start family or classroom arguments.

questions.q: What practical school does this book teach first?
questions.a: The Hanafi school.

questions.q: Should pupils mix isolated rulings to avoid responsibilities?

questions.q: What should you do with a detailed personal legal question?

journeys.title: How Fiqh Guides Our Actions
journeys.aim: We practise responsible use of legal terms and respect for the established Sunni schools.

lessons.title: Fard, Wajib, Sunnah: Using Legal Words Carefully
story: At the academy, a younger pupil asked why some lessons said Fard and others Wajib. Akhlaq remembered several labels but worried that a wrong answer might confuse the child. Instead of guessing, he brought the class textbook to Sheikh Uncle.

They made a chart with Fard, Wajib, Sunnah, Mustaḥabb, Mubāḥ, Makrūh and Ḥarām. “These words are not interchangeable,” the teacher explained. “But they also do not become a game in which you compete to know the most difficult label.” The children used examples that had already been verified in their course, leaving uncertain cases for a scholar.

Mohsina asked about an action in Salah that had been missed. Akhlaq nearly decided the prayer must be repeated immediately. Imaan reminded him that Chapter 35 would teach different consequences for different omissions. They wrote “ASK WHAT WAS MISSED” instead of “START OVER.”

The teacher praised the cautious approach. Good Fiqh begins with accurately identifying the question and the school being taught. The children learned that a short correct answer was often safer than a long confident guess.

teaching.text: Chapter 22 preserves the original Taʿleem-ul-Islam’s Hanafi categorisation of acts and rulings. For study, Fard and Wajib are distinct in Hanafi technical usage, while other schools may use the terms differently. Sunnah and Mustaḥabb refer to recommended practice in their contexts; Makrūh may itself be subdivided in Hanafi instruction. Ḥarām refers to what is forbidden. Knowing categories can assist worship, but a label cannot replace evidence and the relevant circumstances. For a missed act within Salah, the correct response depends on whether it is an essential element, a Wajib act or a Sunnah, and whether the omission was deliberate or forgetful. Those consequences must be taught accurately by a qualified instructor.

questions.q: Are Fard and Wajib always interchangeable in Hanafi Fiqh?
questions.a: No. The school uses a technical distinction.

questions.q: Does Sunnah mean an action is meaningless?
questions.a: No. The Prophetic way has great importance.

questions.q: Should children issue fatwas based on a card game?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What makes a legal answer reliable?
questions.a: Evidence, correct classification, context and qualified explanation.

reflect: When do I use an impressive religious term without being certain what it means?

lessons.title: A Case Is More Than a One-Line Ruling
story: The academy held a discussion about three people preparing for prayer: one was healthy, one had an injured arm, and one was travelling. “They must all do exactly the same thing,” said a pupil who had memorised the usual method.

Imaan explained that basic duties remain important, but the law also provides concessions in genuine circumstances. Mohsin suggested a list of facts that should be known before answering: Is washing safe? Is water accessible? What type of travel is involved? Which school is being followed?

Sir Zameer added that no student should ask someone to reveal private medical details in front of classmates. A child may learn a principle while the particular person speaks privately to a guardian or scholar. Akhlaq wrote “ordinary rule first; verified exception when applicable” in his notebook.

Later the class saw a dramatic online post claiming that one unusual example could establish a ruling for everyone. Rather than sharing it, the children recorded the missing facts. Their teacher said, “The ability to recognise that more information is needed is itself a form of learning.”

teaching.text: In Chapters 22, 35 and 37 the master book distinguishes ordinary obligations from defined concessions and remedies. A ruling may depend on health, risk, travel, ability, intention, timing and the exact act. The Ḥanafī pathway provides the main instruction; school comparisons should not be shortened into misleading slogans. In an app, a child should never be invited to answer an adult’s individual medical or legal question. Practice screens can instead use fictional, safely limited examples and include “ask a qualified adult” as a correct choice. The goal is legal literacy and responsible conduct, not issuing personal fatwas.

questions.a: A legally recognised concession in appropriate circumstances.

questions.q: Does every difficulty automatically change every ruling?
questions.a: No. The conditions of the concession matter.

questions.q: What should a pupil do with a complex private case?
questions.a: Seek a responsible adult and qualified scholar.

questions.q: Why not use one viral example as a universal rule?

lessons.title: Water, Wells and Real Safety
story: At a school camp, the children found an old covered well beside the garden. Akhlaq wondered if the water could be used for Wudu and if it was safe to drink. Mohsin wanted to lower a cup immediately. Sir Zameer stopped them. The well had no safety information, and nobody was allowed to open it.

In class the next day, the pupils read about water, impurity and traditional well rulings in the master manuscript. They were surprised to see discussions of quantities, changing water and historical ways of dealing with contamination.

Imaan made two headings on the board: “Ritual suitability for purification” and “Safe for human drinking.” The teacher explained that the same water might raise different legal and health questions. Classical descriptions of bucket removal were not a laboratory test, and the existence of a traditional rule did not prove that water met modern health standards.

Akhlaq presented the class’s practical decision: keep the well covered, use the approved water supply and ask appropriate authorities before touching an unknown source. He still wanted to study the history, but curiosity no longer meant taking a risk.

teaching.text: Chapter 24 records the classical Hanafi teaching concerning water and wells, including detailed distinctions between small and large bodies, used water and removal of recognised impurities. Those classifications belong in a historical and juristic context. Clean-looking water is not automatically safe to drink: modern drinking-water safety requires appropriate assessment by competent authorities. Conversely, ordinary soil or a harmless visible stain is not always ritual Najasah. Learners should recognise the separate questions and avoid making clinical or religious decisions from appearance alone. Never encourage collecting or testing unknown water; the chapter is about understanding, not dangerous experimentation.

lessons.title: Growing Up with Ghusl and Privacy
story: The academy announced an optional health and wellbeing workshop. Some pupils were curious; others worried that the lesson would ask them to speak about changes in their bodies in front of friends. Salamah, who was helping organise family learning materials, suggested private question envelopes and separate opportunities to speak with trusted adults.

Imaan asked why the book included Ghusl after Wudu. Dadi Jaan explained that some occasions require the greater ritual purification described in Islamic law. It is important that children approaching puberty learn the basic obligation and method before they need to act on it. “But nobody is entitled to your private bodily details,” she added.

Akhlaq worried that asking about hygiene might make a child seem immature. Salaam reassured him that the responsible question is often the one that prevents confusion later. The class prepared a simple resource card: “Ask a trusted guardian and a qualified teacher for the correct instructions. If you need health advice, speak with a competent healthcare professional.”
The workshop ended without public disclosures. The teacher was pleased: the children had learned the difference between understanding a religious duty and discussing someone else’s body.

teaching.text: Master Chapter 26 teaches the Hanafi obligatory components and Sunnah method of Ghusl, and Chapter 28 covers personal hygiene. At ages 11–12, puberty and its legal consequences may be immediate for some learners; important information should not be withheld solely because of a fixed curriculum age. Explain the basic religious rule and approved method in private, suitable materials, with attention to menstruation and other relevant conditions. Never require pupils to report personal events or demonstrate intimate washing. Disability, injury, uncertainty and medical questions should be referred to appropriate caregivers and qualified professionals. The goal is dignity and competent practice, not anxiety.

lessons.title: Purification: Certainty, Doubt and Concessions
story: Akhlaq had washed carefully before prayer, but then began wondering whether he had missed a small patch of his arm. He almost washed the same place again. Imaan reminded him that he had already completed the normal sequence and had no clear evidence of omission.

Sir Zameer explained that careful worship should not become endless checking. People learn a reliable method, complete it properly, and do not turn every passing doubt into a reason to begin again. Meanwhile Mohsina was wearing a medical support on her wrist. The children did not ask her to remove it so they could investigate whether water could reach the skin.

Sheikh Uncle used the examples to explain the difference between ordinary Wudu, legally permitted wiping over suitable footwear, and special rulings for wounds, dressings or unavailability of safe water. He did not give a universal answer for an injury he had not examined.

At the next prayer, Akhlaq followed the taught method calmly and moved on. Mohsina consulted her parent about the dressing. The team learned that two students can both be sincere while requiring different forms of assistance.

teaching.text: Chapters 25, 27 and 29 distinguish ordinary purification from conditions allowing Masah over qualified footwear, special treatment of dressings or Tayammum. The usual Ḥanafī Wudu method remains the first skill. Particular injury cases cannot be settled by a peer, and harm from washing may require clinical advice as well as a scholarly ruling. Teach learners not to mistake ordinary dirt for ritual impurity or to repeat actions solely because of unsubstantiated doubts. Knowledgeable, compassionate teaching helps prevent distress while protecting valid worship.

journeys.title: Salah During Real-Life Challenges
journeys.aim: We learn how to distinguish essential duties, errors, corrections and lawful concessions.

lessons.title: When Salah Needs Correction
story: During a classroom prayer demonstration, Akhlaq mixed up the practice cards. One card showed a missed Sunnah detail; another described the omission of an essential part; a third concerned a forgotten Wajib act. He placed all three under a sign saying “RESTART EVERYTHING.”

Sir Zameer moved the sign aside. “Learning Fiqh means identifying what happened before deciding the remedy,” he said. He reminded the class that the original book separates Fard acts, Wajib duties, Sunnahs and matters that invalidate Salah. The consequences are not identical.

Imaan suggested a safer activity: instead of letting pupils rule on one another’s private prayers, the class would sort teacher-approved fictional examples. Whenever the scenario lacked enough detail, the correct card would be “ASK FOR GUIDANCE.”

The children also remembered that an error does not prove a person is careless or that their worship has no value. At home, Dadi Jaan encouraged Akhlaq to learn the method calmly rather than turn every small uncertainty into a frightening event. “Accuracy and peace can belong together,” she said. The new sign read: FIND THE TYPE OF ERROR FIRST.

teaching.text: Chapter 35 explains mistakes in Salah and the significance of Sajdah Sahw in Hanafi practice. Not every omission invalidates prayer, and not every error is repaired in the same way. The legal outcome can depend on whether a Fard, Wajib or Sunnah was missed, whether the error was deliberate or forgetful, and its exact point in the prayer. The learner’s purpose is to recognise categories and seek an approved method, not issue an instant ruling about someone else. Do not present the repair of prayer as punishment or reward children for noticing other people’s mistakes.

questions.q: Why classify a missed action?

lessons.title: Learning Sajdah Sahw Without Panic
story: Akhlaq had practised the word “Sahw” many times but thought it meant that any forgotten detail ruined his prayer. Imaan brought two blank instruction cards to their tutor. “Can we write the real method instead of guessing?” she asked.

The tutor showed the class the correct procedure from its approved Hanafi learning guide, with attention to when the prayer required it and when it did not. He explained that memorising a technique without understanding its conditions could be misleading. The pupils practised the sequence only as a guided educational demonstration.

Mohsin wanted the app to flash red every time a child made a simulated error. Sir Zameer objected. A frightening animation could teach children to fear Salah. The team changed it to a calm “review the step” screen, followed by a teacher explanation.

At the end, Akhlaq wrote “My duty is to learn carefully, not to be terrified of mistakes.” He also made room for a real-life question: “What if I cannot remember the exact mistake?” That question belonged to a qualified instructor who could establish the facts rather than a game that generated arbitrary rulings.

teaching.text: Master Chapter 35 contains detailed Hanafi rulings for Sajdah Sahw. This child-facing lesson intentionally does not replace the approved full procedural guide; the correct sequence must be presented in an accompanying verified audio-visual appendix and taught under supervision. A missed Wajib due to forgetfulness is not the same as knowingly omitting it, nor is a missing Fard treated as though it were only a Sahw matter. The meaning of the Sunnah and Fard actions learned in Volume 2 remains important. Keep feedback factual and non-alarming.

questions.q: What should teach its step-by-step method?

questions.q: Is a missed Fard treated identically to a missed Wajib?
questions.a: No.

lessons.title: Following the Imām with Care
story: The mosque announced a community learning day. Imaan and Akhlaq attended with their family. When they arrived, a few worshippers were still joining the congregation. Akhlaq wondered whether he should hurry past people to reach the front row.

Salaam stopped him gently. “We do not gain devotion by pushing,” he said. After the prayer, he explained that the Imām leads and those praying behind follow in the prescribed manner. A person who arrives late must learn how to complete missed units correctly, but a child should not invent the method from watching one hurried example.

Back at the academy, the pupils practised identifying where the leader stood and how to form orderly rows with respect for space and accessibility. Mohsina pointed out that a worshipper with a walking aid needed a clear path. Akhlaq moved a chair and recognised that his practical choice was part of mosque etiquette.

The next week a younger child asked Akhlaq how to make up a missed Rakʿah. This time he showed the child to their qualified teacher rather than improvising a rule. He had learned that not answering immediately can sometimes be the most responsible act.

teaching.text: Chapters 31 and 36 describe Adhān, Iqāmah, congregational worship, following the Imām and the rulings of a latecomer. The educational focus is orderly participation, calm movement and respect. Detailed Hanafi rulings for Masbūq and related cases depend on when a person joins and what has been missed; these should be taught by guided examples rather than guessed from a single diagram. Accessible space and safety are responsibilities, not optional niceties. Avoid commanding children to rush into the prayer or to disclose why they arrived late.

lessons.title: Prayer During Illness, Travel and Hardship
story: A school trip was planned for the following month, and the class created a travel checklist. Akhlaq listed food, a jacket and a prayer timetable. Mohsin asked whether every traveller must pray exactly as at home regardless of distance or circumstances.

Their teacher explained that Islamic Fiqh gives specific rulings for travel and difficulty. Those rules are not a licence to stop praying whenever it feels inconvenient, nor do they mean that a sick person must injure themselves to copy the posture of someone healthy.

Imaan remembered a relative who prayed while seated after surgery. She had once worried that sitting made the prayer less sincere. Dadi Jaan corrected her: sincerity does not require ignoring genuine physical limitations. A qualified scholar can explain what the person must do, with medical input where needed.

The class divided its travel plan into two parts: “What I can prepare” and “What needs adult or scholarly advice.” No pupil was asked to share a medical history. Their teacher concluded that knowing the difference between ordinary comfort and a genuine legal concession is a sign of mature religious learning.

teaching.text: Chapter 37 teaches concessions for illness and travel in the Hanafi framework, including prayer positions and journey-related rulings. The actual classification depends on specific facts. Chapter 29 covers Tayammum when water is unavailable or harmful. Caregivers should seek appropriate medical and fiqh advice before applying an exception, especially for disability, injury, chronic illness or hazardous circumstances. Learning that Islam grants a concession is not a reason for children to shame those who use it or demand personal medical explanations. Detailed distance and duration rules should be taught through checked school-specific materials.

journeys.aim: We examine careful fasting rulings while protecting privacy and valuing mercy and sincere worship.

lessons.title: Fasting: Forgetful, Accidental or Deliberate?
story: Akhlaq was helping prepare a Ramadan learning poster when someone asked a difficult question: “If a person eats by mistake, is every fast automatically broken?” Mohsin had heard three different answers from classmates. Sir Zameer invited the team to open the relevant chapter rather than vote on the most popular response.

They learned that the original text draws distinctions between forgetfulness, accidental acts and deliberate violations. The authentic Hadith about a person eating or drinking forgetfully was especially memorable. Still, the children did not turn the topic into a search for anyone who might have eaten during the school day.

Imaan proposed a learning card: “Describe the act accurately; then ask the qualified teacher about the legal consequence.” Another card said, “Never demand someone’s private health or fasting status.” The teacher approved both.

During the exhibition, a visitor asked a question about medical treatment while fasting. Akhlaq recognised that the case needed more detail and medical advice. He did not pretend that a short children’s worksheet settled a complex contemporary ruling. The display taught accuracy without making anyone ashamed.

teaching.text: Chapter 40 classifies Mufsidaat, Makrūh fasting acts and remedies, including Qadā, Kaffārah and Fidyah. A person who eats or drinks due to genuine forgetfulness is not treated the same as one who deliberately violates a valid Ramadan fast, according to the authentic narration cited in the master. Other accidental cases and medical treatments can involve technical differences requiring more detail. An age 11–12 learner should recognise categories, not memorise a dangerous one-line “all mistakes invalidate” rule. Children should not be compelled to disclose whether or why they fasted.

questions.q: Are forgetful and deliberate eating the same ruling?

questions.q: What is Qadā?

questions.q: What is a Mufsid?

lessons.title: When a Fast Is Missed: Mercy and Responsibility
story: At the school community event, a collection box invited families to support people facing hardship during Ramadan. Mohsina asked why some people did not fast and others later completed missed days. Akhlaq started to list reasons from memory, but Salamah asked him to begin with a more important principle: “We should not require a person to explain their health or home circumstances to strangers.”

The class read that Allah has provided exemptions and that the detailed legal outcomes differ by circumstances. Some people make up missed fasts when able; for certain cases of lasting inability, the juristic discussion turns to Fidyah. Kaffārah is another, more specific legal category, not an automatic payment every time a fast is missed.
When a friend suggested publishing a class table showing who had fasted each day, Imaan declined. “We can learn the rulings without keeping personal worship records,” she said.

Their Ramadan workshop became a question-and-answer display with fictional examples and a note directing families to qualified scholars and medical professionals. Akhlaq discovered that clear legal learning can coexist with protecting people’s dignity.

teaching.text: The master Chapter 40 distinguishes Qadā, Fidyah and Kaffārah and specifies that not every invalidation produces the same consequence. Temporary illness and travel can be governed by makeup rulings; permanent inability may have a different remedy, subject to qualified assessment. The conditions for Kaffārah are particularly precise. A child should not be encouraged to calculate remedies for an adult, pronounce medical advice or assume guilt from an exemption. The source includes old quantities that must not be converted into fixed current currency values without contemporary qualified review. Teach Qur’an 2:185 as a reminder of the divine recognition of hardship, not as permission to disregard obligations.

questions.q: What does Qadā usually refer to in fasting?

questions.q: Is Fidyah always the same as Kaffārah?
questions.a: No, they are different categories.

questions.q: Can children determine another person’s medical exemption?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Should a student reveal family fasting details publicly?

reflect: How do I speak about exemptions without judging the person who uses one?

lessons.title: Iʿtikaf, Vows and Responsible Commitments
story: The mosque announced plans for the last ten days of Ramadan. Mohsin suggested a class contest: whoever promised the longest Iʿtikaf would be declared the most devoted. Dadi Jaan discouraged the idea. Worship is not measured by dramatic promises; the legal meaning of Iʿtikaf depends on intention, place, time and other conditions.

Akhlaq asked whether five minutes of quiet Qur’an reading at home automatically counted as the full Ramadan Sunnah retreat. Salamah explained that the master text distinguishes different kinds of Iʿtikaf. It also teaches a particular Hanafi provision concerning women’s designated prayer space, with differing approaches in other schools.

The children chose a different project: a calm plan for reducing distractions during their daily learning, without presenting it as a legal Iʿtikaf. They could help organise books, support a family member and leave space for prayer.

When Mohsin proposed making a vow to Allah if the event succeeded, Sir Zameer said the class should not invent religious promises. A valid Nadhr has legal consequences; a child who wants to do good can make a realistic, ordinary plan without making a binding vow. The team removed the competition and kept the lesson about responsibility.

teaching.text: Chapter 41 preserves the Ḥanafī distinctions among Wājib, Sunnah Muʾakkadah and Mustaḥabb Iʿtikaf, including conditions, duration and the legal place of retreat. It also discusses Nadhr and cautions against casually making binding vows. The Prophetic example of retreat in Ramadan is established, but the legal classifications cannot be collapsed into a one-minute “challenge.” The Hanafi view includes specific provisions for women’s Iʿtikaf in a designated prayer place; other recognised Sunni schools differ, and comparisons need precise source review. Children should distinguish a voluntary personal study plan from a vowed legal commitment. Adults should make arrangements for family duties, health and accessibility before long retreats.

questions.q: What is Iʿtikaf?

questions.q: Are all periods of Iʿtikaf the same legal category?

questions.q: What is Nadhr?

questions.q: Should children make binding religious vows for game points?

reflect: Do I make promises to impress people rather than to fulfil a genuine responsibility?

journeys.title: Giving, Fairness and Community Trust
journeys.aim: Worship of wealth teaches us honesty, confidentiality, dignity and service.

lessons.title: Zakah: Knowledge, Calculation and Confidentiality
story: The class planned a charitable book drive, but a student wanted to set up a wall listing how much each family could afford to give. Imaan worried that a display would embarrass families who could not contribute. Mohsina suggested measuring books collected rather than ranking households by money.

Sheikh Uncle explained the difference between voluntary charity and the prescribed duty of Zakah. Zakah has conditions about qualifying wealth, the legal threshold and eligible recipients. It is not simply any good deed that happens to involve money. A child should appreciate its purpose while leaving family financial rulings to responsible adults and qualified guidance.

The team wrote a privacy rule: NO FAMILY WEALTH AMOUNTS ON THE NOTICEBOARD. They asked donors to place contributions discreetly and requested an adult to verify that items were suitable for the recipient organisation. Akhlaq helped a younger child understand that the one receiving support deserves respect, not pity.

Later the group reported how many readable books had reached the library, without revealing donors or recipients. The result was a kinder model of accounting: accurate about the project but protective of the people involved.

teaching.text: Chapter 42 teaches Zakah, Niṣāb, ownership, qualifying property, eligible recipients and Ṣadaqat al-Fiṭr through a Hanafi foundation, with verified comparative details where appropriate. For ages 11–12, a learner can understand why legal calculation requires dates, asset types and other financial facts. The student book should not set fixed rupee thresholds or invite children to calculate a household’s binding duty from incomplete data. Recipient eligibility and ownership transfer are juristic questions. Voluntary charity is good, but it is not automatically equivalent to Zakah. Qur’an 9:60 identifies eligible categories, and the ethics of giving include dignity, justice and confidentiality.

questions.q: Is Zakah identical to every voluntary gift?
questions.a: No. It is a prescribed act with legal conditions.

questions.q: What is Niṣāb?
questions.a: A legal minimum threshold relevant to Zakah.

questions.q: Should a child publicly list family wealth?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Who handles real family Zakah calculations?
questions.a: Responsible adults with qualified financial and scholarly guidance.

reflect: How can giving respect the dignity of the recipient?

scenario: A teacher wants a leaderboard ranking families by donations. What alternative would you propose?
decide.feedback: Use voluntary anonymous giving and project-level reporting without ranking families or exposing private information.

lessons.title: Worship Must Protect People’s Rights
story: As the exhibition date approached, the children found that the hall booking had been made for the wrong afternoon. Their class could still use the space if a smaller community group agreed to move. Akhlaq suggested telling that group that the academy had priority, even though nobody had actually promised it.

Imaan read the booking message again. It clearly showed the community group’s reserved time. The team had made an error, and the other group was not obliged to solve it. Sir Zameer asked the children to consider whether a religious project could become a reason to neglect someone else's right.

They apologised, requested an alternative room, and helped the caretakers move tables without blaming them. Some exhibits had to be simplified. Mohsin was disappointed, but he admitted that a successful programme should not rest on taking someone else’s place.

In the closing reflection, Dadi reminded the class that worship extends beyond visible rituals to honesty and fairness. Zakah teaches rights connected with wealth, while Hajj teaches care in crowded places. The same principles should already shape a school hall booking. Akhlaq wrote in his notebook: “A good intention does not excuse an unfair method.”

teaching.text: The master curriculum consistently links ʿIbādah with justice and character. Qur’an 16:90 commands justice and excellence, while 2:197 associates pilgrimage with restraint from quarrelling. Financial worship emphasises the rights of eligible recipients, not self-congratulation. An Islamic learning project should not misuse another person's property, time or privacy. Children can practise truthful communication, repair an administrative mistake and support those with fewer resources. These actions are character applications, not substitutions for the prescribed rites themselves.

questions.q: What should we do after a scheduling mistake?

questions.q: Does kindness replace obligatory worship?

questions.q: What makes a community project trustworthy?

journeys.title: The Holy Cities and Living the Guidance
journeys.aim: Pilgrimage teaches ordered worship, rights of others and the responsibilities we carry home.

lessons.title: Pilgrimage Is Worship, Not a Race
story: The exhibition’s final table displayed two journeys: one showing the principal Hajj locations and appointed days, and another showing the shorter rites of Umrah. Akhlaq had drawn a large arrow pointing from Makkah to Madinah. Imaan pointed out that visiting Madinah is deeply meaningful to Muslims but is not itself one of Umrah’s prescribed acts.

They reviewed the educational example of Tamattuʿ Hajj from their master book, taking care not to label it the only possible type of Hajj. The class then sorted Umrah cards: Ihram, Tawaf, Saʿī, and Halq or Qaṣr as legally applicable. The teacher reminded them that actual pilgrims require current authorised arrangements and qualified Fiqh instruction.

One pupil suggested a game in which the winner would be the one who reached the Black Stone fastest. The group rejected it immediately. Pushing and harming others cannot become a model of devotion. Their alternative was a safety-and-kindness decision challenge: offer room to an elderly person, follow official crowd instructions, and do not mistake an optional action for a condition of worship.
Akhlaq ended the display with a question: “What should change about how I treat people after learning Hajj?” It was the right conclusion for the final journey.

teaching.text: Chapters 43–45 distinguish the obligation of Hajj for those who are able, the ritual sequence and the legally distinct Umrah. Chapter 44 uses a Tamattuʿ example and explicitly cautions against treating it as the only form. Chapter 45 explains Ihram, Tawaf, Saʿī and hair removal or trimming, together with the conditions of each. For ages 11–12, review the order and aims, then introduce the principle that Fard, Wājib and Sunnah classifications differ among schools in specific rites. Qur’an 2:197 demands care with conduct during Hajj. A classroom chart does not substitute for actual pilgrim guidance, medical accommodations, current permits, or scholarly decisions about missed rites.

lessons.title: What We Carry After the Last Lesson
story: The exhibition ended quietly. The children folded their posters and returned borrowed materials. On the wall remained a single sheet of paper headed: WHAT DOES GUIDANCE LOOK LIKE AFTER SCHOOL?

Mohsin wrote “correct information.” Mohsina added “care for people.” Imaan drew a small prayer mat, not as a trophy but as a reminder to prepare and pray properly. Akhlaq wrote “ask before sharing a quotation.”

Sir Zameer invited the team to revisit the three volumes they had studied. Their first journey introduced the foundations. The next helped them understand the forms of worship. Now they could recognise that some religious questions required deeper evidence, appropriate assistance and careful judgment.
Akhlaq admitted that he still had many unanswered questions. “Is that a problem?” he asked. Dadi Jaan answered, “Only if you stop learning or pretend to know what you do not.”

They agreed on one final task: each child would choose a useful habit to practise privately for a week. No scores would be displayed. Imaan planned to listen more patiently. Akhlaq promised to check before quoting. Mohsin would honour shared deadlines, and Mohsina would continue helping classmates learn without embarrassment.
They turned off the hall lights and carried the books home. The real journey was not finished. It was becoming part of their choices.

teaching.text: The 45-chapter master manuscript moves from identity and Imaan to the rules and practices of Islam. This final student synthesis should not imply that a twelve-year-old has mastered legal scholarship. It should affirm core belief, accurate basic worship, responsibility toward people and the habit of returning to qualified evidence. Children can reflect privately on choices, learn repentance and repair, and identify sources of help. Their value is not represented by grades of sincerity, public worship tracking or declarations about another person’s belief. The learning process continues with more advanced study after this age level.

questions.q: What is the purpose of these three junior volumes?
questions.a: To understand and practise guidance according to age and ability.

questions.q: Should a student know all advanced rulings by age twelve?
questions.a: No. Learning continues.

questions.q: What should we do with an uncertain legal question?
questions.a: Seek sound evidence and a qualified teacher.

questions.q: What is one lifelong learning habit?
